terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, characterized dismissively by his trademark baseball cap
terms.why_hard: Reducing 'тип' to neutral 'man' misses the mildly dismissive/disconcerted tone of the observer

proposed.en: the guy in the baseball cap
proposed.ja: ベースボールキャップの男

terms.gloss: conventional social appeal to decorum, 'we are all civilized people here'
terms.why_hard: Could sound clumsy if translated literally rather than as a recognized bourgeois social norm

proposed.en: we are all civilized people here
proposed.ja: 私たちは皆まともな人間のはずだ

terms.gloss: haggling petty-market style, unbefitting a modern high-tech enterprise
terms.why_hard: Missing the sharp contrast Durov is drawing between tech innovation and crude bazaar bargaining

proposed.en: haggling like you're at a bazaar
proposed.zh: 像在小菜场上讨价还价一样
proposed.ja: 市場の露天商のように値切る

terms.gloss: English loanphrase used in corporate jargon for an aggressive negotiator
terms.why_hard: Already borrowed in English in the source; target translations should reflect business negotiation role jargon

proposed.ja: アタックドッグ（攻撃役）

terms.gloss: the 'bad cop' role in good cop/bad cop interrogation dynamics
terms.why_hard: Translating as 'bad investigator' sounds Soviet/literal rather than the universal negotiation idiom 'bad cop'

proposed.ja: 悪徳刑事（バッドコップ）

terms.gloss: Ilya Perekopsky, Durov's close associate and business partner at VKontakte
terms.why_hard: Uninformed translators miss that this refers to an actual recurring co-founder figure, Ilya Perekopsky

terms.gloss: a high-strung, irritable, emotionally unstable neurotic
terms.why_hard: Neurasthenia has an antiquated clinical sense in English; here it serves as an exasperated behavioral label

terms.gloss: the foreign executive negotiating on behalf of an international partner/company
terms.why_hard: Must be kept consistent with the earlier designation 'иностранец' while capturing the specific expat manager status

terms.gloss: bleeding/cutting edge of technology
terms.why_hard: Stilted literalism ('front edge') instead of natural industry parlance

terms.gloss: ironic/reverent epithet for Pavel Durov used by the narrator and the foreign counterpart
terms.why_hard: Needs to balance the slightly sardonic distance of the expat's perception with Durov's actual mythos

terms.gloss: pompously or deliberately placing the cap back on his head like an artifact or crown
terms.why_hard: 'Водрузить' carries mock-heroic or deliberate theatrical weight beyond simple 'put back on'

proposed.en: planted the cap back on his head
proposed.ja: キャップを再び頭に乗せた

terms.gloss: shifting personas rapidly like shuffling cards in a deck
terms.why_hard: Translating as split personality rather than theatrical persona management

proposed.en: personas shuffled like a deck of cards
proposed.zh: 人格像洗牌一样接连切换
proposed.ja: 人格がトランプのカードのように次々と入れ替わる

terms.gloss: second of Durov's behavioral archetypes: brash, pushy businessman
terms.why_hard: Losing the distinct archetypal tripartite structure of Durov's personas described in the scene

terms.gloss: third persona: member of the intellectual class, refined, quick-witted, articulate
terms.why_hard: Crucial Russian cultural concept; rendering as mere 'intellectual' misses the cultural demeanor and St Petersburg subtext

terms.gloss: programmers, software developers
terms.why_hard: Treating it as generic 'coders' without recognizing Durov's engineering elitism hierarchy

proposed.ja: コーダー（プログラマー）

terms.gloss: second-class citizens; expendable supporting staff (marketing, sales, HR)
terms.why_hard: Failing to convey the harsh internal VK caste system Durov cultivated

terms.gloss: social network (referring specifically to VKontakte)
terms.why_hard: In 2013 this was the standard descriptor before 'platform' or 'super-app' became prevalent

proposed.ja: ソーシャルネットワーク

terms.gloss: users, network participants
terms.why_hard: Calque from English 'users' common in 2000s Russian tech slang; distinct from formal 'пользователи'

terms.gloss: the leading Russian social networking service founded by Pavel Durov
terms.why_hard: Deciding brand name orthography across languages (VK vs. VKontakte)

terms.gloss: Freemasons; alluding to Russian conspiracy theories regarding VK's meteoric rise
terms.why_hard: Sounding overly literal if not framed as an absurd popular conspiracy theory typical of RuNet rumors

terms.gloss: FSB / Russian security services operatives (historical Cheka successor)
terms.why_hard: Mistranslating as generic 'spies' or 'police'; loses the menacing post-Soviet state security weight

terms.gloss: co-founder and public face of VKontakte, central subject of the biography
terms.why_hard: Standardizing name transliteration across the book

proposed.ja: パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ

terms.gloss: business rationales, commercial logic/justifications
terms.why_hard: Calque/loanblend typical of corporate Russian; shouldn't sound like philosophical 'reasons'

terms.gloss: Durov's theatrical emotional outburst came to an end
terms.why_hard: Must preserve the psychological portrait of Durov weaponizing narcissism and mood swings in negotiations

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms]

terms.gloss: Classes '1' and '2' (typically 239-1 and 239-2), the elite math-focused tracks within a grade level at School 239
terms.why_hard: Mistaking these numbers for grades/years (1st and 2nd grade) rather than class track designations within the same grade cohort

terms.gloss: A grade level cohort comprising several parallel classes (e.g., all 9th-grade classes)
terms.why_hard: Translating literally as 'parallel' instead of school cohort/grade stream

terms.gloss: Russian transliteration of 'nerds'
terms.why_hard: Flattening tone into generic 'geeks' or failing to contrast it with 'botaniki' later in the passage

terms.gloss: Soviet classified research/defense institutes designated publicly only by a PO Box number (pochtovyy yashchik)
terms.why_hard: Translating literally as 'box institutes' without conveying closed, secret Soviet defense R&D facilities

proposed.ja: 「私書箱」と呼ばれた秘密研究所

terms.gloss: Schoolyard slang for nerds, bookworms, or socially awkward high achievers
terms.why_hard: Translating literally as 'botanists'

terms.gloss: Saint Petersburg Lyceum 239, legendary specialized physics and mathematics secondary school
terms.why_hard: Dropping the famous number or failing to recognize its elite prestige in Russia

terms.gloss: Strong negative-diopter prescription glasses for severe myopia
terms.why_hard: Treating 'minus' as an abstract flaw or disadvantage rather than thick eyeglasses

terms.gloss: Lake Zerkalnoye in Leningrad Oblast, site of a famous pioneer/youth camp often used by elite academic schools
terms.why_hard: Translating the toponym literally as 'Mirror Lake' instead of retaining its proper Russian name

terms.gloss: Were not averse to brawling; were quite willing and able to throw punches
terms.why_hard: Misinterpreting 'ne duraki' literally as 'were not fools to fight'

proposed.en: never backed down from a fistfight
proposed.ja: 喧嘩っ早さでも引けを取らなかった

terms.gloss: Slang nicknames for school courtyards/alleys where students congregated to smoke ('little smoke')
terms.why_hard: Missing the smoking reference and translating literally as 'Little Smoke 1 and 2' without context

proposed.ja: 「一服スポット1」「一服スポット2」と呼ばれる中庭

terms.gloss: Behind the garage boxes; archetypal post-Soviet urban setting for illicit youth fights and smoking
terms.why_hard: Missing the ubiquitous cultural trope of garages as unmonitored teenage trouble zones

terms.gloss: Soviet/Russian police prior to the 2011 renaming to 'Politsiya'
terms.why_hard: Anachronistically translating as modern 'police' or confusing it with military militia

terms.gloss: The 'creative class' / demographic stratum involved in knowledge work, media, and marketing
terms.why_hard: Translating rigidly into sociological jargon rather than the mid-2000s post-Soviet buzzword

terms.gloss: Common Russian civic/patriotic motto ('If not us, who?'), often adopted by elite schools or youth organizations
terms.why_hard: Failing to recognize it as a conventional slogan instilled in students

proposed.ja: 我々がやらねば誰がやるのか？

terms.gloss: Nikolai Durov, Pavel's older brother, genius mathematician and lead technical architect of VK and Telegram
terms.why_hard: Overlooking his central technical role and distinct personality relative to Pavel

proposed.ja: ニコライ・ドゥーロフ

terms.gloss: Lev Mednikov, teacher/director at the Academic Gymnasium where Pavel Durov studied
terms.why_hard: Confusing him with School 239 staff; he ran the rival Academic Gymnasium

terms.gloss: Sergey Rukshin, legendary founder and head of the Youth Mathematics Center at School 239, coach of Perelman and Smirnov
terms.why_hard: Treating him as a generic schoolteacher rather than a world-famous math contest coach

terms.gloss: Math circle / extracurricular competitive Olympiad math center (specifically Rukshin's math circle)
terms.why_hard: Dismissing it as a casual after-school club instead of an elite, grueling training institution

terms.gloss: Competitive math coach preparing students for international mathematical olympiads like athletes
terms.why_hard: Translating simply as 'math teacher', missing the sports-coaching ethos of Russian Olympiad training

proposed.ja: 数学オリンピックのコーチ

terms.gloss: pseudo-values of the consumer society, echoing counter-cultural and intellectual discourse

proposed.zh: 消费社会的虚假价值观
proposed.ja: 消費社会の擬似価値観

terms.gloss: kept my mind unpolluted/clear by avoiding mainstream media
terms.why_hard: A literal translation sounds like personal hygiene rather than mental clarity

proposed.ja: 思考をクリアに保っていた

terms.gloss: the protagonist/subject of a journalistic or biographical piece (Pavel Durov)
terms.why_hard: Could be mistranslated as a moral 'hero' rather than the journalistic subject

terms.gloss: late-Soviet state kindergarten
terms.why_hard: Carries specific institutional grimness, strict routine, and bureaucratic assignment

terms.gloss: officially registered via the Soviet propiska residency system
terms.why_hard: Propiska was a strict administrative residency registry determining access to local state services

proposed.ja: 住民登録（プロピスカ）がされている

terms.gloss: a bowl of semolina porridge, the ubiquitous symbol of Soviet kindergarten misery
terms.why_hard: Missing the Soviet cultural trauma associated with compulsory, lumpy semolina porridge

proposed.ja: 決まり切ったセモリナ粥

terms.gloss: entrance/stairwell of a typical Soviet multi-story apartment block
terms.why_hard: Often rendered merely as 'porch' or 'front door' instead of the grim communal entrance

proposed.ja: アパートのエントランス

terms.gloss: Italian school attended by the Durov brothers when their father taught in Turin
terms.why_hard: Need to understand this refers to Durov's childhood period in Italy (Turin)

terms.gloss: Nikolai Durov as a child prodigy

proposed.en: his brother Nikolai as a child prodigy
proposed.ja: 神童としての兄ニコライ

terms.why_hard: Vague unless recognized as Nikolai's live math demonstrations on Italian national TV (RAI)

terms.gloss: Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species', written here in English in the original text
terms.why_hard: Preserving the original code-switching into English that signals advanced erudition

terms.gloss: shared his storehouse of knowledge/lexicon
terms.why_hard: The word 'thesaurus' is used stylistically in Russian for structured mental knowledge, not just a dictionary

proposed.zh: 倾囊相授自己的知识宝库
proposed.ja: 惜しみなく知識の語彙体系を分かち合った

terms.gloss: kitchen dispute/debate, classic Soviet intellectual tradition of table talk
terms.why_hard: The kitchen was the defining Soviet locus for candid, unsupervised intellectual debate

terms.gloss: first-grader (approx. 7 years old)

notes: «Альфа-ромео»: the game is named after the car brand; the plain established brand form suffices in all three languages, and “the Alfa Romeo game” overtranslates a name readers will recognize.

«ВКонтакте» and ВКонтакте: keep the established brand spelling; for zh add the (VK) gloss once-book-wide rather than folk analogies like 人人网/脸书, which date badly and mislead; ja uses the conventional katakana フコンタクテ, with (VK) added where the quoted-brand form needs a gloss.
«Газпрома»: established Japanese form is ガスプロム (not ガズプロム); zh keeps the Latin name with a short parenthetical descriptor.
«Голден Телеком» / «Голден»: Golden Telecom is a proper company name; a zh calque 金色电信 would read as a description, not the firm, so keep Latin across languages.
«Одноклассниках» / «Одноклассники»: one rendering regardless of Russian case form; zh gets the 同学网 gloss, ja plain katakana without redundant parentheses.
«Централ Партнершип»: established transliteration of the company name; zh needs no 影视公司 appendage since context supplies it.
Андрей Лопатин: ja long vowel ロパーチン matches Russian stressed а; en Andrey/Andrei split settled to Andrei per standard transliteration.
Андрей Рогозов: en settled to Andrey (his own public spelling) while ja/zh are unaffected by the Andrey/Andrei choice.
Архитектор: Durov's forum nickname is treated as a capitalized epithet in en, plain 架构师 in zh, katakana アーキテクト in ja; 建筑师/建築家 wrongly suggest the building profession.
Бертова: the plain surname candidate wins; full-name expansions belong in a character list, not inline.
Гриз: en Gris and ja グリス follow the French nickname pronunciation; Griz/グリズ slavishly follows Cyrillic.
Гришин: the person is Yuri Grishin, so Grinin is a mishearing; ja グリシン avoids the long-vowel グリーシン.
Данила: ja ダニラ without long vowel, standard for this name.
День города: generic event name, not tied to St. Petersburg every occurrence: en City Day, zh 城市日, ja 市制記念日.
Джек Дорси: zh 杰克·多西 is the established Chinese rendering of Jack Dorsey; ja ドーシー is established.
Добромыслов: ja ドブロミスロフ avoids inserting a kana for the non-syllabic м.
Доктор Зло: the Austin Powers character is Dr. Evil in en, ドクター・イービル in ja, 邪恶博士 in zh; inline movie glosses are footnote material and dropped for book-wide consistency.
Дом культуры: en House of Culture is the standard rendering of the Soviet institution; zh 文化宫 and ja 文化会館 are the set equivalents.
Дуров: ja ドゥロフ is the established Japanese rendering of Durov; en/zh plain surname, no Pavel expansion.
Дуров-старший: plain relational rendering in all languages; the (Nikolai) expansion is a one-off gloss, not the standing form.
Зингере: the reference is to the Singer House (Дом Зингера) on Nevsky; en the Singer House, zh 辛格大楼, ja シンガー・ハウス; the café-nickname reading Zinger loses the landmark.

value.finding: In the 2013 biography of Durov (Kozlov's 'Дуров: реальная история «ВКонтакте»'), 'Архитектор' is used as a recurring, semi-ironic honorific for Durov as the singular creative/technical mastermind behind VKontakte's design — evoking both the literal 'software architect' role and a grandiose, demiurge-like status among the team, echoing the Silicon Valley 'genius founder' cliché but coloured by Russian internet culture's cult of Durov as an enigmatic, controlling figure.
value.rationale: Preserved the capitalized epithet-like denotation and its recurring status as a nickname across languages; sacrificed some of the ironic-mythologizing connotation particular to Russian tech-journalism register, which is only partially recoverable via quotation marks/capitalization in translation.

value.finding: ICQ was the pioneering instant messenger (launched 1996 by Israeli company Mirabilis, later AOL) whose name puns 'I Seek You'. In Russia it was universally nicknamed 'аська' (Aska) and by the 2000s was the default chat tool for ordinary internet users, predating social networks like VKontakte; it carried strong nostalgic, everyday connotations of pre-social-network Russian internet life, roughly analogous to how AIM/MSN Messenger is remembered in the West.

rendering.en: ICQ (the instant messenger, nicknamed 'ICQ' or colloquially 'Aska' in Russia)
rendering.zh: ICQ（即时通讯软件，相当于当时俄罗斯版的QQ/MSN）
rendering.ja: ICQ（当時のロシアで主流だったインスタントメッセンジャー）

value.rationale: Preserved denotation (a specific IM client) across all three; sacrificed the intimate diminutive connotation of 'аська' but compensated in zh/ja with a brief explanatory gloss so readers grasp its everyday ubiquity, keeping register neutral/expository as befits a serious biography.

value.finding: Gazprom is Russia's largest state-controlled gas company, a symbol of the state-corporate establishment and the fusion of political and business power in Russia. In the 2013 biography of Durov, mentioning Gazprom evokes not merely an energy firm but the very embodiment of the Kremlin-aligned oligarchic/state elite, contrasted against VKontakte's independent, informal internet-startup culture.

rendering.zh: Gazprom（俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司）
rendering.ja: ガスプロム（ロシア国営天然ガス企業）

value.rationale: Kept the proper name (denotation) intact across all languages since it is a globally recognized brand; added a brief explanatory gloss in zh/ja to preserve the connotation of state-establishment power for readers unfamiliar with Russian corporate landscape, sacrificing some brevity/register neutrality.

value.finding: «ВКонтакте» is Russia's dominant social network, founded in 2006 by Pavel Durov (with brother Nikolai) and often called the 'Russian Facebook' — by 2013 it had tens of millions of users and near-total penetration among Russian youth, carrying connotations of a domestic analog to Facebook with looser moderation and a key role in Russian internet culture. Wikipedia renders it as 'VKontakte' in English, Chinese (VKontakte, 縮寫VK, often glossed as similar to Facebook) and Japanese (フコンタクテ, ВКонтакте, abbreviation VK).

rendering.zh: VKontakte（VK，俄罗斯最大的社交网络）

value.rationale: All three target-language Wikipedias already establish 'VKontakte' as the recognizable Latin brand name, so I keep the brand and add a brief appositive gloss ('Russian Facebook'-style positioning) rather than a footnote; the connotation of domestic dominance is carried by the gloss, while the playfulness of the Cyrillic name 'In Contact' is sacrificed. The Japanese katakana フコンタクテ exists on Wikipedia but for a serious business biography the Latin 'VKontakte' with short gloss reads cleaner and matches the company's own branding.

value.finding: «Одноклассники» (ok.ru) is a Russian social network launched 26 March 2006 by web developer Albert Popkov as a clone of the American Classmates.com — a site for finding former schoolmates; by 1 January 2013 it claimed over 205 million registered users. In 2007–2010 it was VKontakte's main domestic rival and actually outranked it until December 2008, and in 2010 Mail.ru Group (later VK) bought it outright, so for a 2013 Russian reader the name meant both the competitor Durov fought and, after the buyout, a sister asset inside the same holding. The word itself is transparently ordinary Russian for 'schoolmates/classmates', which is why Russian coverage routinely writes it in quotes («в „Одноклассниках“») and older, regionally-flavoured audiences were popularly associated with it; but as a trademark it is never translated in Russian business press. Established foreign usage keeps the Latin transliteration: English Wikipedia uses 'Odnoklassniki' (lit. 'Classmates'), Chinese Wikipedia uses 'Odnoklassniki' with the gloss 直译：“同学”, and Japanese Wikipedia heads the article 'Odnoklassniki, OK.ru（アドナクラースニキ…同級生たちの意味）'.

value.finding: The term is a quasi-proper-noun label for the deal style pioneered by Digital Sky Technologies (DST), the Moscow fund founded in 2005 by Yuri Milner and Grigory Finger, which entered VKontakte's capital in 2007 and later applied the same formula abroad (Facebook in 2009): pay a high, founder-pleasing valuation, take no board seat and no operational control, and paper the deal in short simple contracts rather than the multi-hundred-page instruments typical of Western VC. For a Russian reader of the 2013 biography it evoked Milner's signature 'founder-friendly' pitch that won him stakes in Durov's VK and then in Zuckerberg's Facebook. It is not an established term in English, Chinese or Japanese business vocabulary — English media described the same practice ('no board seat, high valuation') without naming it — so it must travel as a branded label attached to the acronym DST.
value.rationale: All three keep DST as the recognizable brand; English and Japanese retain the capital-D 'Deal' as a named product, sacrificing the Russian insider-jargon flavor for an unfamiliar reader, while Chinese converts the proper noun into 'DST-style deal' (式), trading the branded-name connotation for immediate comprehensibility — the right call since no analogue exists in Chinese venture jargon.

value.finding: Refers to the Singer House (Дом компании «Зингер», also known as Dom Knigi), an iconic early 20th-century Art Nouveau landmark on Nevsky Prospekt in Saint Petersburg. Starting in 2010, Pavel Durov rented top floors and the glass dome of this prestigious building as VKontakte's headquarters, turning 'the Singer' into colloquial shorthand for VK's inner sanctum and corporate nerve center. In Russian locative shorthand ('в Зингере'), it treats the founder's surname directly as the building name.
value.rationale: Preserves historical denotation and recognizable architectural identity across all three languages (using standard Chinese '胜家大楼' for Singer Building/House rather than the phonetic '辛格'). Sacrifices the ultra-terse, informal Russian metonymic shorthand ('in Singer') in favor of clear building designation to prevent confusion with the sewing company or Isaac Singer.

value.finding: «ВКонтакте» (literally 'In Contact', international name VK) is the Russian social network founded in 2006 by Pavel Durov in St Petersburg, initially aimed at Russian university students but quickly becoming the dominant Runet social platform, widely called the 'Russian Facebook'. By 2013 it was synonymous in Russia with everyday social media and music/file sharing, and carried a young, non-conformist, libertarian aura linked to Durov. The abbreviation VK was already common but the full name remained standard.
value.rationale: All three audiences already know the network under its Latin brand name VKontakte, so I keep denotation intact by transliterating rather than translating 'In Contact'; Japanese uses the established katakana form フコンタクテ, and each rendering appends the VK abbreviation as the reader-facing analogue. The trade-off is that the literal Russian pun 'In Contact' is not conveyed, which is acceptable since the brand itself never translates it.

value.finding: Гришин here is Dmitry Sergeevich Grishin (b. 1978), CEO of Mail.ru Group from 2003 and chairman of its board from 2012 — the Moscow internet holding that was VKontakte's largest outside shareholder and Durov's recurring antagonist in 2012–2014. For a Russian reader in 2013 the bare surname carried immediate recognition as 'the Mail.ru boss pressing shareholder claims against VK', not a generic name; the gloss's 'Grinin' is a transliteration slip for this same person. English Wikipedia renders him 'Dmitry Grishin' (his fund is Grishin Robotics); Chinese Wikipedia (Mail.ru article) uses 德米特里·格里申; Japanese Wikipedia has no article, and グリシン must be avoided because it is the standard Japanese word for the amino acid glycine.
value.rationale: Each language keeps the denotation via its established rendering: en and zh follow Wikipedia usage, ja uses グリーシン with a long vowel to avoid the glycine collision of グリシン in a serious business-biography register. Only the Russian reader's instant 'Гришин = Mail.ru' association is sacrificed, and that is recoverable from context or a first-mention gloss ('Mail.ru Group CEO Dmitry Grishin').

value.finding: In the 2013 Russian press around VKontakte and the early Telegram period, «Дуров-старший» overwhelmingly referred to Nikolai Valeryevich Durov (born 1980), the elder brother of Pavel Durov (born 1984), not to their father Valery Semyonovich Durov, a philologist. Russian-language articles about VK sometimes used the phrase as a headline-style shorthand for Nikolai, e.g. CNews-style coverage indexed in Wikipedia search results. The phrase carries a mild journalistic contrast: among the two famous Durov brothers, Nikolai is the older, more reclusive technical mind, while Pavel is the public face. The main risk in translation is not that readers will think of the father—English 'the elder Durov' can theoretically mean father—but that in a book about Pavel, 'elder' may be misread as 'senior' in rank or age-generation rather than 'the older of the two brothers'.

rendering.ja: 兄のニコライ・ドゥーロフ

value.rationale: I sacrificed the compactness of the Russian nickname-like form to prevent ambiguity with the father or with a vague 'senior Durov'. In English, adding the first name once at the point of reference keeps the elder-brother sense clear; Chinese and Japanese already have natural brother-order markers (哥哥 / 兄), so the rendering can stay concise while preserving denotation and a serious biographical register.

Astrum.finding: Astrum is the short form of Astrum Online Entertainment (AOE), a Russian IT holding company founded 5 December 2007 that consolidated the country's leading online-game developers and operators (Nival Online, IT Territory, Time Zero, DJ Games). By late 2008 it was the largest player in the Russian online-games market, controlling over 60% of it, and in 2009 it was acquired by Digital Sky Technologies and folded into Mail.Ru Group as its Mail.Ru Games division. To a Russian reader circa 2013 it connoted the domestic boom in free-to-play MMOs and the consolidation of the Runet gaming industry under Mail.ru. The English Wikipedia confirms it as 'Astrum Online Entertainment,' and the name appears untranslated (Latin script) across markets.

rendering.ja: アストラム・オンラインエンターテインメント

Astrum.rationale: I keep the denotation (the specific holding company) and neutral business register by using the full registered name; I sacrifice local-language domestication, since the Latin-script brand had no established Chinese name and Japanese convention for foreign corporate names is katakana transliteration.

DST.finding: DST stands for Digital Sky Technologies, the investment firm founded by Yuri Milner in 2005, which first invested in Russian internet companies (Mail.ru, VKontakte) before gaining global fame through early stakes in Facebook, Twitter and Groupon. In 2010 the Russian assets were split off as Mail.ru Group while the international fund continued as DST Global. For a Russian reader around 2013, 'DST' connoted Milner's powerful, globally connected money — the fund whose capital flows into VKontakte symbolized both the company's valuation and outside influence over Durov.

rendering.zh: DST（数字天空科技，Digital Sky Technologies）
rendering.ja: DST（デジタル・スカイ・テクノロジーズ）

DST.rationale: English readers can handle the full expansion first, then the bare acronym, preserving exact denotation. Chinese and Japanese keep the romanized acronym (as business media do) with a descriptive gloss; this sacrifices the connotation of Milner-era mystique, which no translation can carry, but retains neutral business-biography register.

DST Deal.finding: The term is a quasi-proper-noun label for the deal style pioneered by Digital Sky Technologies (DST), the Moscow fund founded in 2005 by Yuri Milner and Grigory Finger, which entered VKontakte's capital in 2007 and later applied the same formula abroad (Facebook in 2009): pay a high, founder-pleasing valuation, take no board seat and no operational control, and paper the deal in short simple contracts rather than the multi-hundred-page instruments typical of Western VC. For a Russian reader of the 2013 biography it evoked Milner's signature 'founder-friendly' pitch that won him stakes in Durov's VK and then in Zuckerberg's Facebook. It is not an established term in English, Chinese or Japanese business vocabulary — English media described the same practice ('no board seat, high valuation') without naming it — so it must travel as a branded label attached to the acronym DST.
DST Deal.rationale: All three keep DST as the recognizable brand; English and Japanese retain the capital-D 'Deal' as a named product, sacrificing the Russian insider-jargon flavor for an unfamiliar reader, while Chinese converts the proper noun into 'DST-style deal' (式), trading the branded-name connotation for immediate comprehensibility — the right call since no analogue exists in Chinese venture jargon.

Facebook.finding: Facebook refers to the global social networking service created by Mark Zuckerberg and launched in 2004. In the context of the 2013 Durov biography, it serves as VKontakte's primary foreign model, arch-rival, and benchmark, against which VKontakte's interface, feature set, and independence were continuously measured by Russian tech media, investors, and Durov himself.
Facebook.rationale: Preserved universal brand recognition across all three languages without unnecessary parenthetical glosses or katakana glosses, reflecting how professional business biographies and tech journalism in English, Chinese, and Japanese treat the brand as an established proper noun.

Forbes.finding: Forbes is the U.S. business magazine founded in 1917, known worldwide for billionaire lists and investigative business coverage; its slogan is “The Capitalist Tool.” A licensed Russian edition (Форбс) has been published since April 2004 and by 2013 was a prestige outlet for interviews with Russian entrepreneurs. For a 2013 Russian reader the name evoked international capitalist authority rather than a purely local paper; seeking an interview there signaled elite business status.
Forbes.rationale: Kept the established brand (and book-title orthography in zh/ja) so denotation and prestige register match; did not force “Russian edition of Forbes,” sacrificing that local-licensing nuance for recognizability.

Game Insight.finding: Game Insight is a Moscow-founded (2009/2010) developer and publisher of free-to-play mobile and social games, established by Alisa Chumachenko (ex-VP marketing at Astrum Online Entertainment, the Mail.ru-linked game holding) with Igor Matsanyuk as board chairman. For a Russian reader circa 2013 it was one of the flagship success stories of the post-Mail.ru wave of social/mobile game companies, known for VKontakte/Facebook hits like Resort World, Paradise Island and Mystery Manor. Russian Wikipedia uses the Latin-script name untranslated; Chinese Wikipedia's coverage of the Russian game industry also cites 'Game Insight' in Latin script, and no Japanese article exists, so no established katakana or hanzi form competes with the brand.

rendering.ja: Game Insight（ゲーム・インサイト）

Game Insight.rationale: Denotation and brand identity are preserved exactly: it is a proper company name that Russian, Chinese and English sources all keep in Latin script, so translating or transliterating would break recognizability. For Japanese, the Latin name is kept with a katakana gloss on first mention, matching the register of a serious business biography; nothing of connotation is sacrificed except that first-time readers in zh/ja lose the 'ex-Mail.ru orbit' nuance unless the surrounding text supplies it.

ICQ.finding: ICQ was the pioneering instant messenger (launched 1996 by Israeli company Mirabilis, later AOL) whose name puns 'I Seek You'. In Russia it was universally nicknamed 'аська' (Aska) and by the 2000s was the default chat tool for ordinary internet users, predating social networks like VKontakte; it carried strong nostalgic, everyday connotations of pre-social-network Russian internet life, roughly analogous to how AIM/MSN Messenger is remembered in the West.

rendering.en: ICQ (the instant messenger, nicknamed 'ICQ' or colloquially 'Aska' in Russia)
rendering.zh: ICQ（即时通讯软件，相当于当时俄罗斯版的QQ/MSN）
rendering.ja: ICQ（当時のロシアで主流だったインスタントメッセンジャー）

ICQ.rationale: Preserved denotation (a specific IM client) across all three; sacrificed the intimate diminutive connotation of 'аська' but compensated in zh/ja with a brief explanatory gloss so readers grasp its everyday ubiquity, keeping register neutral/expository as befits a serious biography.

Livejournal.finding: This refers to LiveJournal, officially styled with a capital J, a blogging and social-networking platform known in Russian as «Живой Журнал» or «ЖЖ». By 2013 it was more than a diary host for Russian readers: its blogs, communities, friend lists and comment threads formed a major Runet public sphere used by prominent writers, politicians, activists and organizations. The name therefore connoted the influential Russian blogging ecosystem of the 2000s and early 2010s, not merely an individual online journal.
Livejournal.rationale: All three versions preserve the official brand and its neutral register. English needs no gloss, while Chinese and Japanese add a compact category label to preserve the platform-level denotation and some ecosystem connotation, sacrificing the Russian nickname «ЖЖ» and its local cultural resonance.

Mail.ru.finding: Mail.ru began as a Russian free e-mail service (1998) and by 2010 the investment holding Digital Sky Technologies (DST), controlled by Yuri Milner and Alisher Usmanov, was renamed Mail.ru Group. Around 2013, for a Russian reader, 'Mail.ru' was shorthand for this large internet holding — owner of Odnoklassniki and Moi Mir, the email portal, and the chief corporate rival and would-be acquirer of VKontakte (it later took control in 2014). The name carried weight as the biggest, most capitalised player in the Russian-speaking internet, not just a mailbox. In October 2021 the holding was rebranded VK, so a 2013 biography must keep the period name rather than the current one.
Mail.ru.rationale: Preserves denotation (the holding, not just the email service) and register; keeps the period name Mail.ru rather than the later VK. Sacrifices nothing of the connotation of size/dominance, which the bare brand still carries for readers of all three languages; 'Group/集团/グループ' only disambiguates holding from mailbox.

Mail.ru Group.finding: Mail.ru Group (2010–2021; formerly Digital Sky Technologies, renamed VK in 2021) was the Russian internet holding company that by 2013 owned the Mail.ru portal/email service, Odnoklassniki, ICQ, Agent, and a controlling stake in VKontakte. Around 2013 a Russian reader would hear it as the large, consolidating corporate power of Runet — the 'old guard' commercial internet giant that was gradually absorbing Durov's VK, carrying connotations of bureaucratic corporate control and proximity to Kremlin-friendly investors rather than startup idealism. English, Chinese and Japanese Wikipedias all keep the Latin 'Mail.ru' and translate only the word 'Group' (Mail.ru Group / Mail.ru集团 / Mail.ruグループ), confirming the established renderings.
Mail.ru Group.rationale: Preserves denotation and the period-specific corporate name exactly as each Wikipedia edition already does: the brand token 'Mail.ru' stays in Latin script and only 'Group' is localized, which keeps it distinct from the Mail.ru service itself. What is sacrificed is the untranslatable connotation — the 2013 Russian reader's sense of the company as the looming, conservative absorber of VK — which must be supplied by surrounding narrative context rather than the name.

MoiFacultet.finding: MoiFacultet.ru (МойФакультет) was a Russian student social network launched around 2006 that allowed students and graduates to find classmates, reconnect with peers, and stay in touch. The domain moifacultet.ru redirected (by late 2007) to fakultet.ru, which branded itself 'Факультет.ру – новый способ общения' for students and graduates across Russian regions. It was a direct competitor to VKontakte in the 2006–2007 Russian student social-network space, but never achieved significant scale and is now defunct. No Wikipedia article exists for it in any language.
MoiFacultet.rationale: The project is too obscure and defunct to have any established translation in English, Chinese, or Japanese; no Wikipedia article or conventional rendering exists in any target language. Keeping the transliterated brand name preserves denotation exactly; connotation (a small, forgotten competitor) is lost for all readers but would be equally lost with any alternative. Chinese 'MoiFacultet网' adds a genre marker that is helpful but slightly over-formalizes a dead site; dropping the suffix is cleaner.

MoiFakultet.ru.finding: MoiFakultet.ru ('Мой факультет' / 'My Faculty') was an early Russian university-focused social networking project launched around 2006 to connect students by university department, directly competing with early VKontakte and Studlist.ru before VK expanded beyond students and dominated the market. In Nikolai Kononov's 2012–2013 book 'The Durov Code', it represents one of the short-lived, niche campus web portals that failed to scale as VKontakte did.

rendering.ja: MoiFakultet.ru（モイ・ファクリチェット）

MoiFakultet.ru.rationale: Preserved the exact domain name as the primary technical identifier in all languages, adding explanatory glosses in Chinese and Japanese so readers immediately understand that it was a student-niche networking competitor based on university departments ('faculties').

Porn King.finding: Wikipedia (ru/en) does not document this as a formal alias of Pavel Durov. In the 2013 Russian press biography it is an English Twitter nickname used ironically, not a claim that he ran the porn industry. For a Russian reader then it sat in the same register as other English troll handles: a joke about VK’s lax adult content and Durov’s libertine/libertarian persona, left untranslated on purpose.
Porn King.rationale: Kept the English nickname intact in all three languages so the ironic Twitter flavour is not flattened into a job title; added a brief gloss in zh and ja so readers without that 2010s Runet context still get the mock-boast. Literal translation alone would sacrifice register.

Ritz.finding: In 2013 this is The Ritz-Carlton, Moscow, a 5-star luxury hotel that opened July 1, 2007 on Tverskaya Street, on the site of the demolished Hotel Intourist, directly facing Red Square and the Kremlin — one of Moscow's most expensive hotels, whose Ritz-Carlton Suite was among the world's priciest rooms. For a Russian reader it signaled oligarch-level luxury and power lunches within sight of the Kremlin, crucially distinct from the Paris or London Ritz. (It was renamed The Carlton, Moscow only in 2022, after the period of this biography.) The 'Kremlin view' of the next paragraph depends on this specific Tverskaya location.

rendering.zh: 莫斯科丽思卡尔顿酒店
rendering.ja: モスクワのリッツ・カールトン

Ritz.rationale: Denotation and register (luxury-hotel gravitas) are preserved by using the standard brand renderings; connotation of Moscow power-and-money proximity is carried by explicitly naming the city in all three languages, avoiding confusion with the Paris Ritz — this adds a couple of words over the bare brand name, a small sacrifice in economy. English keeps the parenthetical light since 'the Ritz-Carlton' alone in a Moscow context is common usage.

Roem.ru.finding: Roem.ru is a Russian tech/internet-business news site launched in late 2007, founded by Yuri Sinodov (formerly of Webplanet), with Igor Ashmanov also involved in management. It positioned itself as a 'customer-to-business' outlet where insiders and companies could air grievances and 'insider' stories about the Runet industry, and it won industry awards (ROTOR) for tech/telecom journalism. For a Russian reader in 2013 it connoted a niche but respected trade-press insider outlet covering Runet gossip, deals and personnel, similar to a niche tech-industry blog rather than a mainstream media brand.

rendering.en: Roem.ru, a Russian tech-industry news site
rendering.zh: Roem.ru（俄罗斯互联网行业新闻网站，类似科技圈内部资讯媒体）
rendering.ja: ロシアのIT業界専門ニュースサイト「Roem.ru」

Roem.ru.rationale: Preserved the proper name (denotation) across all languages while adding a brief functional gloss so non-Russian readers grasp its niche trade-press register and insider connotation; sacrificed the specific cultural nuance of its c2b/insider-story identity.

Spotify.finding: Spotify refers to the Swedish freemium music-streaming service founded in 2006 and launched in 2008 as a legal alternative to music piracy. By 2013 it was already a prominent international streaming brand, associated with licensed catalogs, subscriptions, advertising, and disputes over digital rights and royalties; for a Russian reader, its contrast with VK’s largely user-uploaded music ecosystem would have been salient. The consulted sources establish the company and period context, though they do not independently confirm the specific reported clash with VK.
Spotify.rationale: All three audiences recognize the Latin-script trademark, so retaining Spotify preserves denotation, brand identity, and neutral business register. The proposed Chinese addition “声田” is not the established name in the consulted Chinese source and would introduce an unnecessary, potentially misleading gloss.

Tahoma.finding: Tahoma is a specific humanist sans-serif typeface designed by Matthew Carter for Microsoft, bundled since Office 97 and set as the default Windows screen font (2000/XP). In the Durov biography the term appears in his own well-known quote: he set the VKontakte logo in Tahoma in three minutes ('blue, white, grey don't annoy anyone'). For a Russian reader of the 2010s, Tahoma is simply the ordinary Windows system font — a default, unpretentious, mass-market choice, which is precisely the point of the anecdote: the logo was thrown together quickly from standard Windows tools.
Tahoma.rationale: The font name is a proper noun known unchanged to all three audiences, so it is kept in Latin script (denotation preserved exactly); appending 字体/フォント only makes the class explicit for readers who may not know it is a typeface, at a small cost in concision.

\u00ab\u0413\u043e\u043b\u0434\u0435\u04.finding: Это Golden Telecom Incorporated — крупный оператор фиксированной связи, передачи данных и интернет-доступа, работавший в России и СНГ с 1996 года; среди его активов были ранние российские интернет-бренды и сервисы. В 2008 году компания вошла в группу «ВымпелКом», а в 2010 году её российское юридическое лицо было присоединено к «Вымпел-Коммуникациям». Для российского читателя около 2013 года название обозначало узнаваемого крупного оператора эпохи становления коммерческого Рунета, уже поглощённого «ВымпелКомом», но не было синонимом бренда «Билайн».

rendering.ja: ゴールデン・テレコム

\u00ab\u0413\u043e\u043b\u0434\u0435\u04.rationale: Во всех языках сохранены историческое фирменное наименование и привязка к периоду; замена на Beeline или VimpelCom исказила бы денотат. В китайском оставлена употребительная латиница без неустоявшегося буквального перевода, ценой меньшей мгновенной прозрачности для читателя.

\u0414\u043e\u0431\u0440\u043e\u043c\u04.finding: No Wikipedia entry or notable public figure matches this name in connection with Durov/VKontakte; it appears to be a minor named individual (colleague or associate) mentioned only in passing in the biography, likely a real but non-notable employee whose surname is simply given to add authenticity to an anecdote. No special connotation beyond being an ordinary Russian surname (from 'добрая мысль' - good thought), carrying no slang or cultural weight.
\u0414\u043e\u0431\u0440\u043e\u043c\u04.rationale: Preserved denotation via standard transliteration consistent with existing proposals; no connotation or register to preserve since it is a plain proper name with no special resonance.

\u0410\u0440\u0445\u0438\u0442\u0435\u04.finding: In the 2013 biography of Durov (Kozlov's 'Дуров: реальная история «ВКонтакте»'), 'Архитектор' is used as a recurring, semi-ironic honorific for Durov as the singular creative/technical mastermind behind VKontakte's design — evoking both the literal 'software architect' role and a grandiose, demiurge-like status among the team, echoing the Silicon Valley 'genius founder' cliché but coloured by Russian internet culture's cult of Durov as an enigmatic, controlling figure.
\u0410\u0440\u0445\u0438\u0442\u0435\u04.rationale: Preserved the capitalized epithet-like denotation and its recurring status as a nickname across languages; sacrificed some of the ironic-mythologizing connotation particular to Russian tech-journalism register, which is only partially recoverable via quotation marks/capitalization in translation.

\u041a\u043e\u043d\u0441\u0438\u043b\u04.finding: Consigliere is the Mafia counselor title popularized by 'The Godfather' — the advisor who counsels the don but wields no formal power himself. In the 2013 Russian biography of Durov, calling his inner circle 'консильери' is an ironic, pop-culture jab casting Durov as a mob boss and his top managers/advisers as his mafia-style counselors, playing on VKontakte's cult-of-personality and secrecy reputation.

rendering.ja: コンシリエーレ（ゴッドファーザー風の相談役）

\u041a\u043e\u043d\u0441\u0438\u043b\u04.rationale: English keeps the Italian loanword directly recognizable via 'The Godfather'; Chinese uses '军师' (a strategist/counselor trope familiar to Chinese readers) glossed with the Godfather reference to preserve the Mafia connotation since the bare loanword lacks resonance; Japanese keeps the loanword コンシリエーレ, which is already established via Godfather films, with a brief gloss to preserve register in a business biography.

\u0410\u043d\u0434\u0440\u0435\u0439 \u0.finding: Andrey Sergeyevich Lopatin is a St. Petersburg programmer, two-time ACM-ICPC world champion (with Nikolai Durov, 2000–2001), TopCoder Open 2009 winner, and from 2006 coach of the SPbU competitive-programming team. Around 2008 the Durovs brought him into early VKontakte to rewrite and optimize the engine; he later became deputy CTO and in 2012–14 worked on Telegram/MTProto. For a 2013 Russian reader the name meant elite olympiad-coder pedigree, not a generic hire.

rendering.ja: アンドレイ・ロパーチン

\u0410\u043d\u0434\u0440\u0435\u0439 \u0.rationale: EN follows the existing English Wikipedia form Andrey (not Andrei) so readers can look him up; ZH and JA keep phonetic name-only renderings already proposed, without titles, matching a serious biography’s first mention of a person. Competitive-programming fame is left to surrounding prose.

\u0417\u0438\u043d\u0433\u0435\u0440\u04.finding: Refers to the Singer House (Дом компании «Зингер», also known as Dom Knigi), an iconic early 20th-century Art Nouveau landmark on Nevsky Prospekt in Saint Petersburg. Starting in 2010, Pavel Durov rented top floors and the glass dome of this prestigious building as VKontakte's headquarters, turning 'the Singer' into colloquial shorthand for VK's inner sanctum and corporate nerve center. In Russian locative shorthand ('в Зингере'), it treats the founder's surname directly as the building name.
\u0417\u0438\u043d\u0433\u0435\u0440\u04.rationale: Preserves historical denotation and recognizable architectural identity across all three languages (using standard Chinese '胜家大楼' for Singer Building/House rather than the phonetic '辛格'). Sacrifices the ultra-terse, informal Russian metonymic shorthand ('in Singer') in favor of clear building designation to prevent confusion with the sewing company or Isaac Singer.

\u00ab\u0410\u043b\u044c\u0444\u0430-\u0.finding: In the 2013 Durov/VK biography this is not a car dealership or a pun but the title/subject of Nikolai Grishin’s first computer game, which he sold at a Saratov software stall: a game about cars branded after the Italian maker. For a Russian reader the quoted hyphenated form «Альфа-ромео» is the usual magazine spelling of Alfa Romeo, an exotic sporty European marque; italics or quotes mark it as a product name rather than running prose. It carries no slang and no extra cultural joke beyond ‘a game about flashy Italian cars.’
\u00ab\u0410\u043b\u044c\u0444\u0430-\u0.rationale: Kept the internationally standard brand denotation and a slightly elevated product-name register; gave up the Russian quotes/hyphen and any need to gloss that it was a game title, which the surrounding sentence already states.

\u0414\u0443\u0440\u043e\u0432-\u0441\u0.finding: In the 2013 Russian press around VKontakte and the early Telegram period, «Дуров-старший» overwhelmingly referred to Nikolai Valeryevich Durov (born 1980), the elder brother of Pavel Durov (born 1984), not to their father Valery Semyonovich Durov, a philologist. Russian-language articles about VK sometimes used the phrase as a headline-style shorthand for Nikolai, e.g. CNews-style coverage indexed in Wikipedia search results. The phrase carries a mild journalistic contrast: among the two famous Durov brothers, Nikolai is the older, more reclusive technical mind, while Pavel is the public face. The main risk in translation is not that readers will think of the father—English 'the elder Durov' can theoretically mean father—but that in a book about Pavel, 'elder' may be misread as 'senior' in rank or age-generation rather than 'the older of the two brothers'.

rendering.ja: 兄のニコライ・ドゥーロフ

\u0414\u0443\u0440\u043e\u0432-\u0441\u0.rationale: I sacrificed the compactness of the Russian nickname-like form to prevent ambiguity with the father or with a vague 'senior Durov'. In English, adding the first name once at the point of reference keeps the elder-brother sense clear; Chinese and Japanese already have natural brother-order markers (哥哥 / 兄), so the rendering can stay concise while preserving denotation and a serious biographical register.

\u00ab\u0412\u041a\u043e\u043d\u0442\u04.finding: «ВКонтакте» is Russia's dominant social network, founded in 2006 by Pavel Durov (with brother Nikolai) and often called the 'Russian Facebook' — by 2013 it had tens of millions of users and near-total penetration among Russian youth, carrying connotations of a domestic analog to Facebook with looser moderation and a key role in Russian internet culture. Wikipedia renders it as 'VKontakte' in English, Chinese (VKontakte, 縮寫VK, often glossed as similar to Facebook) and Japanese (フコンタクテ, ВКонтакте, abbreviation VK).

rendering.zh: VKontakte（VK，俄罗斯最大的社交网络）

\u00ab\u0412\u041a\u043e\u043d\u0442\u04.rationale: All three target-language Wikipedias already establish 'VKontakte' as the recognizable Latin brand name, so I keep the brand and add a brief appositive gloss ('Russian Facebook'-style positioning) rather than a footnote; the connotation of domestic dominance is carried by the gloss, while the playfulness of the Cyrillic name 'In Contact' is sacrificed. The Japanese katakana フコンタクテ exists on Wikipedia but for a serious business biography the Latin 'VKontakte' with short gloss reads cleaner and matches the company's own branding.

\u0414\u0443\u0440\u043e\u0432.finding: Павел Валерьевич Дуров (род. 1984), российский программист и предприниматель, основатель и глава «ВКонтакте»; к 2013 году — главный герой книги, фигура культового статуса в русском интернете: «русский Цукерберг», вегетарианец-либертарианец, эпатажный и скрытный. Самостоятельное «Дуров» — стандартный русский журналистский приём повторного упоминания героя после первого полного представления; фамилия несла ауру молодого гения и бунтаря. Неоднозначность лишь с братом Николаем Дуровым, сооснователем VK, поэтому единообразие ссылки критично.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ
\u0414\u0443\u0440\u043e\u0432.rationale: All three targets keep the standard surname-only reference consistent with each language's established convention (English press 'Durov'; Chinese Wikipedia 杜罗夫; Japanese Wikipedia ドゥーロフ with long vowel, correcting the proposed ドゥロフ). Denotation and register fully preserved; only the Russian-specific celebrity aura is not carried by the bare name and must come from context.

\u041a\u0430\u0437\u0430\u043d\u0441\u04.finding: This is the Cathedral of Our Lady of Kazan on Nevsky Prospekt in Saint Petersburg, built 1801–1811 by Andrei Voronnikhin, with its famous semicircular 96-column colonnade facing the avenue. For a Russian reader it is one of the city's most recognizable landmarks, standing directly opposite the Singer House (Дом книги), a spot every Petersburg resident knows; in a 2013 Durov/VK narrative it functions purely as a geographic anchor on Nevsky Prospekt. In Soviet times it housed the Museum of Religion and Atheism, and Kutuzov's tomb is inside, but none of that cultural depth is likely needed — the reference is locational. The name derives from the Kazan Icon of the Mother of God, not the city of Kazan, which matters because naive transliterations ('Kazan city cathedral') would be wrong.
\u041a\u0430\u0437\u0430\u043d\u0441\u04.rationale: All three renderings are the established standard names in their language editions and among guidebooks, so denotation, the landmark connotation and neutral register all carry over intact; nothing meaningful is sacrificed, except that a reader unfamiliar with Saint Petersburg won't automatically know it sits on Nevsky Prospekt opposite Singer House — that must come from surrounding context, not the name itself. Chinese Wikipedia also uses 喀山主教座堂, but 喀山大教堂 is the prevailing simplified-Chinese form and matches the proposal.

\u0410\u043d\u0434\u0440\u0435\u0439 \u0.finding: Andrey Olegovich Rogozov (b. 1987) is a VKontakte insider: per Russian Wikipedia he joined the company in 2007 as a developer and by 2017 became its general director; around 2013 he was a lead developer/executive director, one of Durov's earliest technical lieutenants. To a Russian reader of a 2013-era biography he connotes the small founding-era St. Petersburg engineering core that built VK alongside Durov. His 'главный разработчик' title is best rendered as 'lead developer' (en), 首席开发者/首席工程师 (zh), and 首席開発者 or チーフエンジニア (ja).

rendering.ja: アンドレイ・ロゴゾフ

\u0410\u043d\u0434\u0440\u0435\u0439 \u0.rationale: Name renderings follow the established transliteration standards (Andrey, not Andrei; 安德烈; アンドレイ) and match the team's prior segments, preserving denotation; the neutral register suits a business biography, and the title is handled consistently as 'lead developer' rather than over-promoting him to an executive title he only gained later.

\u0412\u041a\u043e\u043d\u0442\u0430\u04.finding: «ВКонтакте» (literally 'In Contact', international name VK) is the Russian social network founded in 2006 by Pavel Durov in St Petersburg, initially aimed at Russian university students but quickly becoming the dominant Runet social platform, widely called the 'Russian Facebook'. By 2013 it was synonymous in Russia with everyday social media and music/file sharing, and carried a young, non-conformist, libertarian aura linked to Durov. The abbreviation VK was already common but the full name remained standard.
\u0412\u041a\u043e\u043d\u0442\u0430\u04.rationale: All three audiences already know the network under its Latin brand name VKontakte, so I keep denotation intact by transliterating rather than translating 'In Contact'; Japanese uses the established katakana form フコンタクテ, and each rendering appends the VK abbreviation as the reader-facing analogue. The trade-off is that the literal Russian pun 'In Contact' is not conveyed, which is acceptable since the brand itself never translates it.

\u0414\u0436\u0435\u043a \u0414\u043e\u0.finding: Джек Патрик Дорси (р. 19 ноября 1976, Сент-Луис) — американский предприниматель и программист, сооснователь Twitter (2006) и Square/Block. Русская Википедия и российские СМИ 2013 года знают его именно как сооснователя и главу Twitter, кумира стартап-сцены; в биографии Дурова он служит западным аналогом-визави основателя соцсети. Все справочные издания подчёркивают, что Twitter создан им совместно с Ноа Глассом, Бизом Стоуном и Эваном Уильямсом — упрощение до «создателя» принадлежит исходному тексту, а не фактам.
\u0414\u0436\u0435\u043a \u0414\u043e\u0.rationale: Имя — устоявшаяся транскрипция в каждом языковом сообществе (en/zh/ja Википедии подтверждают), поэтому сохраняется денотация и регистр без изменений; атрибуцию «создатель Twitter» оставляю на совести исходного текста и не сглаживаю в самом имени, при необходимости переводчик абзаца может добавить «co-founder» в глагольной конструкции. Жертвую лишь возможностью встроить уточнение в само имя — это невозможно для персоналии.

\u00ab\u041e\u0434\u043d\u043e\u043a\u04.finding: Prepositional-case mention of «Одноклассники» (Odnoklassniki, lit. 'Classmates', later OK/OK.ru), the Russian social network launched by Albert Popkov in March 2006 around finding former school classmates. By 2013 it was VKontakte's main domestic rival, owned by Mail.ru Group, with tens of millions of users (VK had overtaken it as Russia's most popular social network in late 2008). For a Russian reader of 2013 the everyday word 'classmates' and the brand are fused, so the name instantly signals 'the other big social network, slightly older-skewing, classmate-reunion flavored'.

rendering.en: Odnoklassniki (a Russian social network whose name literally means "Classmates")
rendering.ja: オドノクラスニキ（Одноклассники、ロシアのSNS）

\u00ab\u041e\u0434\u043d\u043e\u043a\u04.rationale: All three renderings keep the transliterated brand (denotation) as each Wikipedia edition already does; en and zh add a gloss of the literal meaning or category so the classmate connotation and rival-network status survive, while the parenthetical apparatus is dropped on later mentions — sacrificing some of the Russian wordplay where name and ordinary noun coincide.

\u0413\u0440\u0438\u0448\u0438\u043d.finding: Гришин here is Dmitry Sergeevich Grishin (b. 1978), CEO of Mail.ru Group from 2003 and chairman of its board from 2012 — the Moscow internet holding that was VKontakte's largest outside shareholder and Durov's recurring antagonist in 2012–2014. For a Russian reader in 2013 the bare surname carried immediate recognition as 'the Mail.ru boss pressing shareholder claims against VK', not a generic name; the gloss's 'Grinin' is a transliteration slip for this same person. English Wikipedia renders him 'Dmitry Grishin' (his fund is Grishin Robotics); Chinese Wikipedia (Mail.ru article) uses 德米特里·格里申; Japanese Wikipedia has no article, and グリシン must be avoided because it is the standard Japanese word for the amino acid glycine.
\u0413\u0440\u0438\u0448\u0438\u043d.rationale: Each language keeps the denotation via its established rendering: en and zh follow Wikipedia usage, ja uses グリーシン with a long vowel to avoid the glycine collision of グリシン in a serious business-biography register. Only the Russian reader's instant 'Гришин = Mail.ru' association is sacrificed, and that is recoverable from context or a first-mention gloss ('Mail.ru Group CEO Dmitry Grishin').

\u00ab\u0426\u0435\u043d\u0442\u0440\u04.finding: Central Partnership (often abbreviated as CP / ЦПШ) is one of the largest film production and distribution companies in Russia, founded in 1996 and part of Prof-Media (later Gazprom-Media). In the context of early-2010s VKontakte, it was one of the foremost major copyright holders and film studios actively confronting VK over massive copyright infringement and unlicensed movie hosting.

rendering.ja: セントラル・パートナーシップ

\u00ab\u0426\u0435\u043d\u0442\u0440\u04.rationale: Central Partnership is the official and international English trade name chosen by the Russian studio itself. For Chinese and Japanese readers, providing the transliteration/semantic translation alongside the international Latin brand name preserves both immediate legibility as a major rights-holder studio and accurate corporate denotation.

\u00ab\u041e\u0434\u043d\u043e\u043a\u04.finding: «Одноклассники» (ok.ru) is a Russian social network launched 26 March 2006 by web developer Albert Popkov as a clone of the American Classmates.com — a site for finding former schoolmates; by 1 January 2013 it claimed over 205 million registered users. In 2007–2010 it was VKontakte's main domestic rival and actually outranked it until December 2008, and in 2010 Mail.ru Group (later VK) bought it outright, so for a 2013 Russian reader the name meant both the competitor Durov fought and, after the buyout, a sister asset inside the same holding. The word itself is transparently ordinary Russian for 'schoolmates/classmates', which is why Russian coverage routinely writes it in quotes («в „Одноклассниках“») and older, regionally-flavoured audiences were popularly associated with it; but as a trademark it is never translated in Russian business press. Established foreign usage keeps the Latin transliteration: English Wikipedia uses 'Odnoklassniki' (lit. 'Classmates'), Chinese Wikipedia uses 'Odnoklassniki' with the gloss 直译：“同学”, and Japanese Wikipedia heads the article 'Odnoklassniki, OK.ru（アドナクラースニキ…同級生たちの意味）'.

rendering.en: Odnoklassniki — first mention only: Odnoklassniki (“Classmates”), the rival network Mail.ru later folded into the same holding; thereafter Odnoklassniki or OK.ru
rendering.zh: Odnoklassniki — 首次出现加注：Odnoklassniki（俄语音译，意为“同班同学”）；此后一律作 Odnoklassniki 或 OK.ru
rendering.ja: アドナクラースニキ（Odnoklassniki、ロシア語で「同級生たち」の意）— first mention; thereafter アドナクラースニキ or Odnoklassniki

\u00ab\u041e\u0434\u043d\u043e\u043a\u04.rationale: All three keep the brand as a brand (denotation, and the corporate-legal weight it carries in a business biography), adding a one-time literal gloss so the reader can hear the everyday Russian word 'schoolmates' and hence the 2000s nostalgia-and-provincial-audience connotation; the gloss is dropped after first mention, so the flavour is sacrificed in running text in exchange for a consistent trademark form. For Japanese the earlier proposal オドノクラスニキ is rejected in favour of アドナクラースニキ, the transliteration already established in Japanese-language sources (од- → アド-, reflecting Russian unstressed /a/).

\u041a\u0443\u0437\u044f.finding: В русской Википедии нет статьи, связывающей Василия Бабича с этим прозвищем, поэтому его роль раннего программиста «ВКонтакте» независимо подтвердить не удалось. «Кузя» обычно является уменьшительной формой имени Кузьма, но с именем Василий морфологически не связано; здесь это личное прозвище или сетевой ник. Для русского читателя около 2013 года оно звучало фамильярно, мягко и слегка по-детски, контрастируя с технической ролью разработчика.
\u041a\u0443\u0437\u044f.rationale: Во всех трёх языках сохранены денотация и статус индивидуального прозвища посредством транслитерации. Уменьшительно-фамильярный русский оттенок частично утрачивается, но его искусственная замена местным ласкательным именем исказила бы личность и была бы неуместна в серьёзной биографии.

\u0413\u0440\u0438\u0437.finding: «Гриз» — школьное прозвище директора гимназии, где учился Дуров; это не фамилия, а кличка, которую, судя по контексту биографии, директор получил за сходство с испанским художником-кубистом Хуаном Грисом (Juan Gris) либо за суровые, «серые» черты внешности или характера. Для русского читателя 2013 года это звучало как типичная школьная кличка: слегка ироничная, обиходная, обозначающая персонажа из школьного фольклора, а не официальную фигуру. Прямых источников о самом директоре не найдено, поэтому этимология остаётся вероятной, но не доказанной.
\u0413\u0440\u0438\u0437.rationale: Preserved the nickname's sound and its phonetic identity with the painter Juan Gris (zh standard translit 格里斯 exists, but for a nickname 格里兹 is acceptable and consistent); sacrificed the ironic schoolyard connotation, which a pure transliteration cannot carry without a footnote. All three languages keep it capitalized as a nickname, signaling it is not a surname.

\u041a\u0430\u0437\u0430\u043d\u0441\u04.finding: In Petersburg speech this elliptical adjective means Kazan Cathedral (Казанский собор / Cathedral of Our Lady of Kazan) on Nevsky Prospect, the Voronikhin neoclassical church facing the Singer House, not the city of Kazan or Moscow Kazansky Station. For a 2013 Russian reader it is a landmark of central St Petersburg, Kutuzov’s tomb and 1812 military glory, used as a geographic shorthand for that stretch of Nevsky.
\u041a\u0430\u0437\u0430\u043d\u0441\u04.rationale: Preserved denotation with the established full names each language already uses for this church; sacrificed the elliptical Petersburg nickname that would read as the Tatar city or a railway station.

\u0411\u0435\u0440\u0442\u043e\u0432\u04.finding: Это женская форма русской фамилии Бертов; в книге ею названа одноклассница Дурова из Академической гимназии, близкая школьная подруга и практикующая айкидо. Отдельной статьи о ней в русской Википедии нет, а доступные справочные материалы о Дурове и книге не устанавливают её полное имя или общепринятое иностранное написание. Для русского читателя фамилия нейтральна и лишь грамматически указывает на женщину; специальных культурных коннотаций она не несёт.
\u0411\u0435\u0440\u0442\u043e\u0432\u04.rationale: Сохранены денотация, женская форма фамилии и нейтральный биографический регистр; использованы обычные для каждого языка способы передачи русских фамилий. Точное авторское латинское написание установить не удалось.

\u0414\u043e\u043a\u0442\u043e\u0440 \u0.finding: Это русское имя Dr. Evil — главного злодея комедийной серии «Остин Пауэрс», сыгранного Майком Майерсом и пародирующего прежде всего бондовского Блофельда. Для российского читателя 2013 года прозвище вызывало образ узнаваемого карикатурного суперзлодея: эксцентричного, самодовольного и театрально претендующего на мировое господство. Применительно к Дурову это ироническая самоподача, а не буквальная характеристика его как злого человека.
\u0414\u043e\u043a\u0442\u043e\u0440 \u0.rationale: Во всех трех языках использованы закрепившиеся имена персонажа, сохраняющие денотацию и комически-злодейскую коннотацию. Японский вариант заменяет буквальное ドクター・イービル на принятое в названии персонажа Dr.イーブル; часть русской интонации прозвища при этом неизбежно утрачивается.

\u0414\u0430\u043d\u0438\u043b\u0430.finding: In Nikolay Kononov's biographical book 'The Durov Code' (2012–2013), 'Данила' appears as a given name / online handle representing a competitor or participant in the early Russian social networking sphere (associated with rival platform forums / staff). As a standard Russian male given name (a colloquial and canonical variant of Daniil), it functions straightforwardly as a personal identifier rather than a coded cultural meme, though to Russian readers it carries the informal, youthful tone typical of early RuNet tech and community forums.
sources: Н. В. Кононов. «Код Дурова. Реальная история “ВКонтакте” и ее создателя». М.: Манн, Иванов и Фербер, 2012.
\u0414\u0430\u043d\u0438\u043b\u0430.rationale: Preserved the phonetic proper name and standard transliteration conventions across English, Chinese (standard Xinhua transliteration), and Japanese katakana. Sacrificed the mild domestic/informal nuance of the Russian hypocoristic/variant form relative to 'Daniil', as proper names in non-fiction biographies require direct phonetic rendering.

\u0414\u043e\u043c \u043a\u0443\u043b\u0.finding: Дом культуры (ДК) is the standard Soviet/Eastern-bloc club institution: a state- or trade-union-run community center for 'cultural leisure' — concerts, cinema, hobby circles, amateur theatre and sports — deliberately counterposed to 'cultureless' leisure like drinking and hooliganism. In a 2013 Russian biography, a ДК near the school reads as an unremarkable, slightly dated municipal fixture of any town or district, carrying a faint official-Soviet overtone but still neutral everyday vocabulary rather than ironic or ideological.
\u0414\u043e\u043c \u043a\u0443\u043b\u0.rationale: All three keep the denotation of a public community cultural center and its slightly institutional register; they drop the specifically Soviet/state-run flavor, which is unavoidable since no Western term carries the same history — 'House of Culture' preserves the calque for English, while 文化宫/文化会館 give the target audiences their own familiar analogue.

\u00ab\u0413\u043e\u043b\u0434\u0435\u04.finding: «Голден» is the everyday Russian shorthand for Golden Telecom (по-русски «Голден Телеком»), a US-registered telecom and internet-services provider that operated in Russia 1996–2010 and was acquired by VimpelCom (Beeline) in 2007. It was one of the oldest primary providers in the Runet, ran its own fibre backbone and Moscow Wi-Fi network, and in the 2000s was among the large operators whose hosting/transit capacity early VKontakte relied on. To a 2013 Russian reader it was a familiar, slightly informal name for a major infrastructure player — not a metaphor for 'golden'. The proposed renderings 'Golden' / 'ゴールデン' / 'Golden' drop the Telecom element and sound like the English adjective, losing the denotation entirely.

rendering.ja: ゴールデン・テレコム

\u00ab\u0413\u043e\u043b\u0434\u0435\u04.rationale: I restore the full company name so the denotation (a named telecom/provider firm, not a 'golden' metaphor) is preserved for every audience; the informal shorthand register is given up, which is unavoidable in a serious biography, and Chinese additionally gets a bracketed translation as the firm has no established Chinese name.

\u00ab\u0413\u0430\u0437\u043f\u0440\u04.finding: Gazprom is Russia's largest state-controlled gas company, a symbol of the state-corporate establishment and the fusion of political and business power in Russia. In the 2013 biography of Durov, mentioning Gazprom evokes not merely an energy firm but the very embodiment of the Kremlin-aligned oligarchic/state elite, contrasted against VKontakte's independent, informal internet-startup culture.

rendering.zh: Gazprom（俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司）
rendering.ja: ガスプロム（ロシア国営天然ガス企業）

\u00ab\u0413\u0430\u0437\u043f\u0440\u04.rationale: Kept the proper name (denotation) intact across all languages since it is a globally recognized brand; added a brief explanatory gloss in zh/ja to preserve the connotation of state-establishment power for readers unfamiliar with Russian corporate landscape, sacrificing some brevity/register neutrality.

\u0414\u0435\u043d\u044c \u0433\u043e\u0.finding: In Russian civic usage День города is the named annual municipal festival of a given city, typically timed to its founding anniversary, with official ceremonies, street concerts and fireworks. For Saint Petersburg it is fixed on 27 May, the 1703 founding of the Peter and Paul Fortress, and is listed among the city’s official commemorative dates. A 2013 Petersburg reader would hear a specific public holiday and mass outdoor programme, not an ordinary day spent in town.
\u0414\u0435\u043d\u044c \u0433\u043e\u0.rationale: Kept the conventional short festival name (denotation of a civic holiday). Dropped an explicit ‘Petersburg’ gloss and Japanese 市制記念日, which wrongly implies municipal-charter day rather than founding-day festivities.

Twitter.finding: Twitter is the American microblogging and social networking service founded in 2006 (renamed X in 2023). For a Russian reader in 2013 it was the prominent Western counterpart and competitor to VKontakte: a global, English-centric platform used by tech elites, journalists and opposition activists, associated with the 2011–2012 protest mobilization ('Twitter-revolutions'). Russian usage transliterated it as «Твиттер», keeping the foreign brand name rather than translating it, which signaled a cosmopolitan, foreign-tech connotation.
Twitter.rationale: All three renderings keep the globally recognizable brand (denotation) and add the established local name (推特, ツイッター) once for accessibility, matching how each Wikipedia edition presents it; the Russian-specific connotation of a foreign rival to VK is contextually recoverable and not encoded in the name itself, so nothing is forced. Register stays neutral, fitting a business biography.

Vanity Fair.finding: Vanity Fair is Condé Nast's American monthly of popular culture, fashion and current affairs, founded 1913, folded into Vogue in 1936 and revived in 1983 under Graydon Carter's long editorship (1992-2017); for a 2013 reader it signalled glossy, high-prestige celebrity-and-power journalism. The 'New Establishment' issue it is referenced for is Vanity Fair's annual autumn ranking (published from 2010) of the most influential people in technology, media, finance and Hollywood - i.e. inclusion meant being certified as part of the new global power elite, which is exactly the frame a Russian reported biography would use for a young internet founder like Durov. The name is a proper title, not a translatable phrase: Russian press and Russian Wikipedia keep the Latin 'Vanity Fair' (only glossing it parenthetically as «Ярмарка тщеславия», the Thackeray/Bunyan allusion), so the Russian reader met the English brand, not a translated one. The Chinese and Japanese audiences already know it by settled conventions: 名利场 and ヴァニティ・フェア respectively.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Crowley and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Dubuc (attest the annual 'New Establishment List', 2010-2014)
Vanity Fair.rationale: Keeps the established brand-name convention in each language and the formal, uninflected register of a business biography, giving up nothing on denotation; the only loss is the Russian reader's faintly ironic awareness of the title as «Ярмарка тщеславия», which is not carried in the source text itself and should not be re-added. In Chinese and Japanese the 杂志 / 誌 suffix marks it as a periodical on first mention so no reader mistakes it for the novel.

Zynga.finding: Zynga was the pioneer and dominant titan of social gaming on Facebook around 2009–2012, famous for FarmVille, CityVille, and aggressive viral growth mechanics. In the context of the 2013 Durov/VKontakte biography, it represents the Silicon Valley blueprint for monetizing social networks through third-party browser games and in-app currency, directly mirrored in the RuNet by VK's gaming platform and clones like 'Schastlivy Fermer' (Happy Farmer).
Zynga.rationale: Zynga is a globally recognized proper noun in the tech industry, requiring no annotation in English. In Chinese and Japanese business prose, glossing the official localized corporate name upon first mention (星佳 in Chinese; ジンガ in Japanese) preserves clarity and formal register for readers who remember its local branch or news coverage from the early 2010s.

units.en: “First they hate us, then they start loving us,” Durov answered, shouting over the clatter of the train cars. A metallic voice announced “Kropotkinskaya,” and the companions pushed their way to the doors. Emerging unscathed from the subway, they crossed the square and walked down the alleyways running down to the Moskva River, toward the hall hosting HighLoad++.
units.zh: “起初他们会恨我们，然后就会爱上我们，”杜罗夫扯着嗓子，盖过车厢哐当的轰鸣声回答道。机械的播音腔报出了“克鲁泡特金站”，两人随即挤向车门。完好无损地走出地铁后，他们穿过广场，沿着向下蜿蜒至莫斯科河的小巷，阔步走向举办HighLoad++大会的会场。
units.ja: 「最初は嫌われても、そのうち愛されるようになるさ」と、ドゥーロフは電車のガタゴトという軋み音を怒鳴り声でかき消しながら答えた。無機質なアナウンスが「クロポトキンスカヤ駅」を告げ、二人はドアに向かって人波をかき分けた。地下鉄から無傷で抜け出ると、広場を渡り、モスクワ川へと下る路地を抜けて、HighLoad++カンファレンスが開催されているホールへと足を速めた。

units.en: His old acquaintance Bunin had invited VKontakte (VK) to talk about how they optimized for high loads on their servers. About 20 million people visited the network every day. Seeing the programmers packed shoulder to shoulder waiting for his speech, Illarionov forgot about the haters, ran through his talk in his head, and took the microphone.
units.zh: 老相识布宁邀请VKontakte（VK）来做分享，讲讲他们是如何优化服务器的高负载的。当时该社交网络每天有约2000万人访问。看到程序员们摩肩接踵、挤得水泄不通地等着他的演讲，伊拉里奥诺夫把黑粉们抛到了脑后，在心中快速过了一遍发言大纲，拿起了麦克风。
units.ja: 旧知のブニンが、サーバーにかかる高負荷をどう最適化しているか話してほしいとVKontakte（VK）を招いたのだった。このSNSには1日に約2000万人が訪れていた。彼の登壇をぎっしり肩を寄せ合って待つプログラマーたちを目にしたイラリオノフは、ヘイターたちのことなど忘れ、頭の中で発表の流れを反芻し、マイクを握った。

units.en: The most scandalous reform at VKontakte (VK) began when Durov, pacing hands-in-black-trousers past the orange juice machine and the cowhide couch, came up with his next provocation. He carried it gingerly to the door behind which Illarionov was sitting, and insinuatingly said to him: “What if we make all the walls public?”
units.zh: VKontakte（VK）史上最富争议的改革始于这样一幕：杜罗夫双手插在黑裤兜里，在鲜榨橙汁机和奶牛花纹沙发前踱着步，构思出了又一场挑衅。他小心翼翼地把这个念头带到了伊拉里奥诺夫办公室门前，轻声细语地对他说：“要是把所有的个人留言墙全部公开，怎么样？”
units.ja: VKontakte（VK）史上最も物議を醸した改革は、ドゥーロフが黒いズボンのポケットに手を突っ込み、オレンジジュースの自販機と牛柄のソファの横を歩き回りながら、新たな挑発を思いついたことから始まった。彼はそのアイデアを壊れ物のように大切に抱えてイラリオノフの座る部屋の扉まで運び、甘い声で囁きかけた。「なぁ、すべてのウォールを一般公開したらどうだろう？」

units.en: A council of war was immediately convened, headed by his brother Nikolai, who deemed the idea insane. “The only thing you’ll accomplish is mass unrest and an exodus to other social networks!”
units.zh: 他们立刻召集了一场会议，由哥哥尼古拉主持。尼古拉认为这个主意简直疯了：“你唯一能达到的效果，就是引发群体愤怒，大家集体出逃到其他社交网站去！”
units.ja: 兄のニコライを筆頭に直ちに協議の場が持たれたが、ニコライはそのアイデアを狂気の沙汰だと切り捨てた。「お前がこれで手にするのは、大規模な暴動と他のSNSへのユーザー流出だけだぞ！」

units.en: Yet Durov stood firm—he wasn’t reinventing the wheel; Facebook had pulled off a similar stunt, and nothing had happened, everyone had swallowed it. The world was becoming more open; people needed to be trained in the transparency of intentions and actions. Everything you write, and everything friends have written on your wall, should be visible to others. Restricting it was an option. But by default—it should be open.
units.zh: 然而杜罗夫态度坚决——他并不是无中生有，Facebook早就搞过类似的名堂，结果什么事也没有，大家全照单全收了。世界正在变得越来越开放；应当让人们习惯于意图和行为的透明化。你自己写的一切，以及朋友们在你的留言墙上写下的内容，都应该展示给其他人看。想限制访问可以自己设，但在默认状态下——必须公开。
units.ja: しかしドゥーロフは断固として譲らなかった。自分が車輪の再発明をしているわけではない、Facebookも同様の変更を行って何事もなく全員がそれを受け入れたではないか、と。世界はより開かれた場所になりつつある。人々は意図や行動の透明性に慣れさせねばならない。自分が書いたものも、友人がウォールに書き残したことも、すべて他人に公開されるべきなのだ。非公開に制限することはできてもいい。だがデフォルトでは、公開にしておくべきなのだ。

units.en: Behind the innovation lay not just religious faith, but a desire to draw people deeper into interactions with other users. VKontakte (VK) was thereby boosting its engagement, which was already the highest in Europe—users were already spending hours on Durov’s platform every single day.
units.zh: 这项创新的背后，不仅有一种类似宗教般的狂热信念，更有拉动人们更深介入彼此互动的渴望。VKontakte（VK）借此进一步推高了本就冠绝欧洲的用户参与度——用户每天在杜罗夫的地盘上一泡就是几个小时。
units.ja: この新施策の背後にあったのは、宗教的信念だけではなく、他のユーザーとの相互作用へ人々をより強く巻き込みたいという欲求だった。これによりVKontakte（VK）は、ただでさえ欧州一を誇っていたエンゲージメントをさらに高めることになった。ユーザーは毎日何時間もドゥーロフのサービスに入り浸っていたのである。

units.en: Despite fierce pushback from Nikolai, Kuzya, and the others, Durov held his ground. The coders developed the new wall, and on August 2, it was unveiled to the network.
units.zh: 尽管遭到了尼古拉、库佳和其他人的激烈反对，杜罗夫依然一意孤行。程序员们开发出了新版留言墙，并在8月2日正式向全网推出。
units.ja: ニコライやクージャらの激しい抵抗にもかかわらず、ドゥーロフは自説を押し通した。プログラマーたちが新たなウォールを開発し、8月2日に全ネットに向けて公開された。

units.en: The Totem had underestimated the users. Just as he had predicted a few years before, a VKontakte (VK) page had become a person’s second self. The meddling was taken as an assault on private life.
units.zh: “图腾”低估了用户。正如他几年前所预言的那样，VKontakte（VK）的主页已经成了人的“第二副人格”。这次改动被人们视为对个人私生活的蓄意侵犯。
units.ja: 「トーテム」はユーザーを甘く見ていた。彼が数年前に予言した通り、VKontakte（VK）のプロフィールページは人間の第二のペルソナとなっていたのだ。この仕様変更は、プライバシーへの侵害と受け取られた。

units.en: “Durov is a scumbag,” “You violated my privacy,” “Put everything back the way it was,” people wrote. The sector of the public brain responsible for folklore spawned a meme: “Woke up this morning, looked around—and Durov rearranged all the furniture in my room!”
units.zh: “杜罗夫是个混蛋”、“你侵犯了个人隐私”、“恢复原样”，人们纷纷怒骂。网民大脑中负责生成民间段子的中枢孕育出了一个网络热梗：“今早一睁眼，好家伙——杜罗夫把老子房间里的家具全给调换了位置！”
units.ja: 「ドゥーロフのクズ野郎」「プライバシーの侵害だ」「元に戻せ」と人々は書き立てた。庶民のフォークロアを生み出す脳細胞が、あるミームを誕生させた。「朝起きて部屋を見渡したら、ドゥーロフが部屋の家具を全部勝手に並べ替えたみたいになってた！」
